meta.title: Who really said "Let food be thy medicine and medicine be thy food"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Hippocrates gets the credit, but the line appears nowhere in the Hippocratic Corpus. Two peer-reviewed studies call it a misquotation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Let food be thy medicine and medicine be thy food'?
meta.ogDescription: The line is absent from the Hippocratic Corpus — scholars call it a misquotation. Here's what Hippocrates' texts actually say about food.

answer.label: Not Hippocrates — no such line in his corpus
answer.authorDates: No documented author · the sentence is absent from the Corpus Hippocraticum
answer.sourceLine: No source exists. The line appears nowhere in the sixty-odd treatises of the Hippocratic Corpus, and the two peer-reviewed studies that went looking for it — Cardenas (2013) and Witkamp & van Norren (2018) — both conclude there is no evidence Hippocrates ever wrote or said it.

source.heading: What the Hippocratic texts actually say

docMeta.dd: None — the sentence is absent from the Corpus Hippocraticum
English rendering by Diana Cardenas (2013); the Greek original is long out of copyright
Diana Cardenas, “Let not thy food be confused with thy medicine: The Hippocratic misquotation,” e-SPEN Journal 8, no. 6 (2013): e260–e262

source.excerpt: Ἐν τροφῇ φαρμακείη ἄριστον, ἐν τροφῇ φαρμακείη φλαῦρον, φλαῦρον καὶ ἄριστον πρός τι. — rendered by Cardenas as “In food excellent medication, in food bad medication, bad and good relatively.”
trail: Wikiquote files the sentence under its Disputed section ↗, noting it “is often attributed to Hippocrates but does not appear in the Hippocratic corpus,” and pointing to Diana Cardenas’ study as the source of that finding.

The peer-reviewed position is the same. A 2018 review in the European Journal of Pharmacology begins: “There is no evidence that Hippocrates, although being credited for it, ever literally stated” the phrase — PubMed record, PMID 29936236 ↗.
Cardenas’ own reasoning is reproduced at length by Science-Based Medicine ↗, which adds that the line is “nowhere to be found in the more than 60 texts known as The Hippocratic Corpus.”
The one passage that comes close, On Aliment §XIX, survives in Greek at Greek Wikisource ↗ — and says food may be either excellent or bad medication, which is not the slogan.
source.excerptNote: This is not the famous line — no text containing that line has ever been found. This is the passage from On Aliment §XIX that Cardenas proposes as the possible root of the confusion, and it says something close to the opposite: food can be excellent medication or bad medication, good and bad only relative to circumstance. Cardenas also notes the treatise is now dated to the Hellenistic period rather than to Hippocrates.

source.rightsNote: No copyright status can honestly be asserted for the popular English sentence, because it has no identified author, work, or first-publication date. The ancient Greek of On Aliment is long in the public domain; the short English rendering shown above is Diana Cardenas’, from her 2013 e-SPEN Journal article, and is reproduced here as a brief attributed quotation.

author.name: Hippocrates
author.kicker: About the man who gets the credit
author.heading: Hippocrates
author.metaLine: c. 460 – c. 370 BC · Greek physician, traditionally the “Father of Medicine”
author.bio: Hippocrates of Kos is remembered as the physician who insisted diseases had natural rather than divine causes, and who built medicine around careful observation of the patient. The body of writing that carries his name — the Corpus Hippocraticum — was almost certainly assembled from many hands over several generations; Wikipedia notes the question of whether Hippocrates wrote any of it “has not been conclusively answered.” Diet and regimen genuinely mattered enormously to Hippocratic medicine, which is exactly why a food slogan sticks to his name so easily — but the famous sentence is not his.

misattribution.heading: Where the credit goes wrong
misattribution.intro: This may be the single most-shared line ever pinned on Hippocrates, and nobody has produced a text for it. Three separate things get confused here — the wording, the sentiment, and one genuine passage that sounds a little like both.

items.why: Wikiquote places the sentence under Disputed and states that it “is often attributed to Hippocrates but does not appear in the Hippocratic corpus” — see Wikiquote ↗. A 2018 review in the European Journal of Pharmacology is blunter still: “There is no evidence that Hippocrates, although being credited for it, ever literally stated” it — abstract on PubMed ↗.

Diet mattered enormously in Hippocratic practice, but Cardenas argues the slogan reverses the actual doctrine: “Hippocratic doctors clearly saw a difference between food and medicines” — food was assimilated into the body’s substance, a medicine changed the body’s nature without becoming part of it. Quoted in full at Science-Based Medicine ↗.

Cardenas names one cryptic line in On Aliment as a possible root of the confusion — and notes that this text is nowadays attributed to the Hellenistic period, though Galen in antiquity treated it as Hippocratic. The Greek survives at Greek Wikisource ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: No Greek text, no translation, no pre-modern printing: the honest answer is that the author of this sentence is unknown, and that it is not Hippocrates — the position taken by Wikiquote ↗ and by every scholar who has looked.

context.heading: Why this one matters
lead: This is not a meme that stayed in the meme layer. The sentence has been printed in the medical literature itself: a 2004 BMJ editorial by Richard Smith, archived at PubMed Central ↗, opens by noting a reviewer of folic acid science closing his piece “by quoting Hippocrates” with exactly this line. Once a claim clears peer review it stops being checked, and the phrase has since travelled through nutrition papers, supplement marketing, and wellness copy with an ancient physician’s name welded to it.

That is Cardenas’ actual complaint. Her argument, quoted at length by Science-Based Medicine ↗, is that Hippocratic doctors drew a sharp line the slogan erases: food was material the body assimilated and turned into itself, while a medicine was something that altered the body’s nature without becoming part of it. The misquotation does not merely misattribute a nice thought — it puts a conflation into Hippocrates’ mouth that Hippocratic writers specifically refused.
detailsBody: The “Hippocrates said” framing is shakier than it looks even for lines that are in the corpus. Wikipedia’s article on Hippocrates ↗ notes that because of the variety of subjects, styles and apparent dates, the Corpus could not have been written by one person, and that the volumes were probably produced by his students and followers.

The closest genuine text, On Aliment, is a case in point: Cardenas notes it is now attributed to the Hellenistic period, though Galen in antiquity took it for Hippocrates. So even the near-miss passage that may have seeded the confusion is not securely his.
context.pull: Hippocratic doctors clearly saw a difference between food and medicines.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists "Let food be thy medicine and medicine be thy food" in its Disputed section, stating it is often attributed to Hippocrates but does not appear in the Hippocratic corpus, citing Diana Cardenas' 2013 e-SPEN Journal article and quoting the Greek of On Aliment (Περί τροφής) §XIX.

Same as above, confirmed against the raw wikitext: section heading '== Disputed ==' and the entry text including the Greek «ἐν τροφῇ φαρμακείη ἄριστον, ἐν τροφῇ φαρμακείη φλαῦρον, φλαῦρον καὶ ἄριστον πρός τι» and the note that Cardenas in turn cites Jacques Jouanna.

David Gorski (June 1, 2015) writes that the quote 'is thought to be a misquote, as it is nowhere to be found in the more than 60 texts known as The Hippocratic Corpus', and quotes Cardenas verbatim: Hippocratic doctors clearly saw a difference between food and medicines; food was assimilated and converted into the body's substance while a medicine changed the body's nature; a possible root of the confusion is the cryptic phrase in On Aliment, 'In food excellent medication, in food bad medication, bad and good relatively', a text nowadays attributed to the Hellenistic period but considered Hippocratic in antiquity by Galen.
The Greek text of the Hippocratic work Περί τροφής, section XIX, reads: 'Ἐν τροφῇ φαρμακείη ἄριστον, ἐν τροφῇ φαρμακείη φλαῦρον, φλαῦρον καὶ ἄριστον πρός τι.'

PubMed record PMID 29936236 — Witkamp RF, van Norren K, 'Let thy food be thy medicine….when possible', Eur J Pharmacol. 2018 Oct 5;836:102-114 — whose abstract opens: 'There is no evidence that Hippocrates, although being credited for it, ever literally stated "let thy food be thy medicine and thy medicine be thy food".' Confirmed by fetching this record through NCBI E-utilities (https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=pubmed&id=29936236&rettype=abstract&retmode=text), as the rendered HTML view is cookie-gated to automated clients.

Richard Smith, 'Let food be thy medicine…', BMJ (2004), notes that Mark Lucock ends his review of folic acid science by quoting Hippocrates with this line — an instance of the misattribution appearing in a major medical journal.

Hippocrates lived c. 460 – c. 370 BC and is traditionally called the 'Father of Medicine'; the Hippocratic Corpus could not have been written by one person and was probably produced by his students and followers, and whether Hippocrates authored any treatise in it 'has not been conclusively answered'.

Bibliographic details of the Cardenas paper: Diana Cardenas, 'Let not thy food be confused with thy medicine: The Hippocratic misquotation', e-SPEN Journal, vol. 8, issue 6, pages e260-e262, 2013, DOI 10.1016/j.clnme.2013.10.002. Verified against the Crossref registration record (the publisher's own pages at sciencedirect.com and clinicalnutritionespen.com return 403 to automated fetches).
